tldr: This paper identifies the mismatches that occur when pairing a pretrained whole-body tracking policy with a runtime safety filter (CBF). It introduces CoFiT, a filter-aware fine-tuning method that adapts the policy to the filter by supplying constraint observations, temporal feedback, and targeted penalty rewards.
hero_caption: Comparison of whole-body reaching motions under an active safety filter. A conventional fine-tuning baseline (left) suffered from severe conflicts between filter interventions and reference tracking, requiring an emergency stop in 5 out of 10 trials. In contrast, CoFiT (right) adopted a cooperative avoidance posture and successfully completed all 10 trials.
overview:
When deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, reference trajectories from teleoperators or motion generators often lack obstacle information. A popular modular approach applies a safety filter based on Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) downstream of a reinforcement learning (RL) whole-body tracking policy to prevent collisions.

However, designing the tracking policy and safety filter independently causes severe problems on hardware. When the filter overwrites torques or joint commands, the robot experiences dynamics and state distributions unseen during training. Reference tracking then clashes with safety avoidance, causing violent chattering, oscillations, and falls.

The authors systematically analyze the mismatches arising at this policy–filter interface across three axes: dynamics, objective, and information. Based on these insights, they develop CoFiT (Constrained Filter-aware Tuning), a fine-tuning method that teaches tracking policies to coordinate with runtime filters. CoFiT passes constraint directions and margins derived inside the safety filter to the policy as action-space observations. It also provides historical feedback of past interventions and penalizes constraint relaxations, training the policy to anticipate filter actions and execute smooth whole-body motions.

Experiments in simulation (on TWIST2 and SONIC) and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid show that CoFiT substantially reduces constraint violation time compared to baseline methods. It dramatically suppresses excessive filter corrections and aggressive vibrations. Notably, on hardware, where the baseline violently oscillated and required operator emergency stops in half the trials, CoFiT completed every trial smoothly and safely.
contributions: Systematically categorized the dynamics, objective, and information mismatch mechanisms that emerge when operating whole-body tracking policies independently of downstream safety filters.

Proposed CoFiT, a fine-tuning method that feeds compact action-space constraint boundaries from the safety filter back into the policy, harmonizing them via temporal feedback and dedicated alignment rewards.
Demonstrated substantial reductions in constraint violation time and achieved smooth, oscillation-free whole-body motion in both simulation and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid.

sections.heading: Can a Handy Safety Filter Make a Humanoid Go Wild?
sections.summary: Placing a safety filter (CBF) downstream of an RL tracking policy offers an appealing modular design. However, designing them independently pushes the policy into unfamiliar states when the filter intervenes, triggering balance loss and violent oscillations.
sections.details:
Safely operating humanoids in human environments like homes or warehouses requires respecting geometric constraints, such as obstacles, while preserving whole-body dynamic balance. Modern humanoid control commonly uses a two-stage approach: a motion generator provides reference trajectories, and an RL-trained tracking policy maps them to whole-body joint commands.

The challenge is that the reference trajectory often ignores environmental obstacles and safety constraints. To avoid these at runtime, practitioners frequently place a Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety filter downstream of the tracking policy. The filter intervenes only when necessary to minimally modify commands. This seems like a great way to handle new obstacles without retraining the policy.

However, this independent design has a major trap. When the safety filter intervenes, the policy experiences this correction as an endogenous disturbance that was never seen during training, driving it into out-of-distribution states. Consequently, the robot loses whole-body balance, and a tug-of-war between the tracking policy and the filter causes violent oscillations. This paper uncovers the root causes behind these failures as three core mismatches and introduces CoFiT, a fine-tuning method that enables policies to cooperate smoothly with existing filters.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Safety Filter Learning and Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on RL with safety filters and constraint handling across bipedal and humanoid control hierarchies. Most existing methods either treat the filter and policy separately or train from scratch, leaving the adaptation of pretrained trackers to runtime filters unexplored.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans two areas: learning in the presence of safety filters and enforcing constraints across humanoid control hierarchies.

### II-A Learning with safety filters
Approaches that integrate safety filters into RL training (such as CBF-RL or Safety Filtering While Training) introduce penalties for filter interventions into the reward function, encouraging policies to choose intervention-free actions. However, these methods do not address how to adapt an already capable, pretrained whole-body tracking policy to a runtime filter, nor what constraint representations and feedback interfaces should be provided.

### II-B Constraints across the control hierarchy
For quadrupeds and humanoids, safety constraints have been applied at various levels, including planners, high-level reference modifiers, and whole-body controllers (WBC). Task-space CBFs, such as ConstrainedMimic, solve a quadratic program (QP) to compute corrective torques while accounting for contact forces and posture tasks. Even in these systems, the upstream tracking policy and downstream safety filter are typically designed in isolation. This paper directly targets the policy–filter interface.

sections.heading: How Safety Filters Work: Relative Degree Two CBFs and Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: This section covers the formulation of relative degree two CBFs for position constraints under torque control and task-space QP filters that compute minimal torque corrections while maintaining contact consistency. CoFiT adapts tracking policies to this fixed runtime filter.
sections.details:
### III-A Relative Degree Two Control Barrier Functions
Safety constraints are formulated as state constraint functions $h_i(z) \geq 0$. For position constraints under torque control, the control input torque appears only after taking the second derivative through acceleration, making them relative degree two. In this setting, an intermediate barrier $h_{2,i}$ that incorporates both the barrier value and its rate of approach is used to directly regulate how quickly the system nears the constraint boundary.

### III-B Whole-Body Constrained Tracking
A humanoid safety filter cannot simply minimize raw torque changes. Disregarding ground reaction forces can disrupt foot contacts and cause the robot to fall. Therefore, this work adopts the task-space QP filter framework from ConstrainedMimic, which penalizes deviations in contact forces, task accelerations, and posture accelerations via weights $W_t$.

CBF inequality constraints are formed into matrix inequalities $G_{i,t} \tau \leq b_{i,t}$ using distances between robot bodies and obstacles. The filter solves a QP that includes actuator torque limits and a slack variable $\delta_t^*$ to prevent infeasibility. The resulting filtered torque $\tau_t^\mathrm{F}$ is converted back into joint target commands and sent to the robot. The goal of this research is to adapt the policy's commands without modifying this fixed runtime filter.

sections.heading: Why Plug-and-Play Filters Fail: The Three Mismatches
sections.summary: This section breaks down the failure modes of independently designed tracking policies and safety filters through three key mechanisms: dynamics mismatch, objective mismatch, and information mismatch.
sections.details:
### IV-A Dynamics Mismatch
While the filter intervenes to preserve safety, the policy views these corrections as endogenous disturbances. As seen in Figure F2 (4.80–5.62 s), when the filter alters torques to avoid a torso collision, the policy reacts to this unexpected motion by pitching forward and lifting a knee. This inadvertently changes the contact mode, introducing support dynamics uncertainty and further degrading balance. When facing multiple obstacles sequentially, posture recovery motions collide with subsequent constraints, compounding instability.

### IV-B Objective Mismatch
When a reference trajectory intersects an obstacle, the tracking policy continuously tries to push through toward its goal, while the filter pushes back to enforce safety. This persistent conflict produces violent chattering and vibrations. Even if the policy trains on filtered transitions, commands that push lightly against an obstacle yield the exact same filtered outcome as commands that push aggressively into it. As a result, the policy has no incentive to reduce interventions. Rewards must explicitly penalize filter corrections and QP slack (constraint relaxation).

### IV-C Information Mismatch
Even with appropriate penalties, a policy cannot avoid constraints if it lacks the information needed to select safe actions. Without knowing whether an obstacle lies to the left or right, the policy's output distribution remains identical until an intervention actually happens. The policy needs to observe barrier distances, approach velocities, and the constraint normals in its action space before the constraint becomes active.

sections.heading: Designing CoFiT: See, Remember, and Align with Constraints
sections.summary: CoFiT provides compact action-space constraint observations (normals and margins) derived from the QP, feeds back past correction history, and fine-tunes the policy using penalty rewards for corrections, constraint violations, and slack.
sections.details:
### V-A Constraint-Context Observations
To inform the policy about upcoming constraints, the QP filter's internal inequalities are mapped into the action space (the PD target space). By substituting the torque mapping $\tau = B_t a + c_t$, action-space constraint normals $v_{i,t}$ and margins $\beta_{i,t}$ are obtained. Combining these with the barrier value $h_i$ and its Lie derivative $L_f h_i$ produces a compact normalized observation vector $o^\mathrm{c}_{i,t}$. The constraint with the minimum barrier value (the most critical one) is embedded into feature $e_t$ using a lightweight MLP. This requires no expensive differentiation, directly reusing the QP's byproducts.

### V-B Temporal Feedback and Policy Integration
To handle dynamics shifts from filter interventions, observations include the previous filter correction $\Delta a_{t-1} = q_{t-1}^\mathrm{cmd} - q_{t-1}^\mathrm{prop}$ and the executed filtered action $\widetilde{a}_{t-1}$. In addition, a 10-step history of these signals and the constraint embedding $e_t$ is injected into the policy's first hidden layer. The newly added weights are zero-initialized, ensuring training starts from the exact behavior of the pretrained tracking policy.

### V-C Policy–Filter Alignment Rewards
To discourage the policy from provoking filter interventions and to prevent the QP from relying on constraint relaxations, three penalty terms are added to the base tracking reward:
- Filter correction penalty $r_t^\mathrm{c}$: Penalizes task-space torque modifications.
- Uncorrected action constraint violation penalty $r_t^\mathrm{r}$: Encourages proposed actions to satisfy CBF conditions prior to filtering.
- Slack penalty $r_t^\mathrm{s}$: Penalizes the QP constraint relaxation slack (the degree of infeasibility).
These rewards guide the policy to generate safe trajectories that naturally avoid interfering with the filter.

sections.heading: Thorough Validation in Simulation and on the Unitree G1 Hardware
sections.summary: Extensive evaluations were conducted, including a 29-variant ablation on sphere scenes, diverse household scenes, and hardware reaching tasks on the Unitree G1. CoFiT cut constraint violation time by up to 91% and completed all hardware runs without emergency stops.
sections.details:
Evaluations used several key metrics: Violation Time percentage, Correction RMS, Residual Acceleration and Command Total Variation (Command TV) for smoothness, and Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE) for tracking accuracy.

### VI-A Controlled Design Study on Sphere Scenes
A controlled ablation study across 29 designs on sphere obstacles revealed that constraint information is effective only when both the action-space normal $\hat{v}$ and margin $\hat{\beta}$ are provided. Providing this compact representation led to faster training and fewer violations than feeding full world-frame obstacle coordinates. Adding correction history and the slack penalty also contributed directly to reducing violations.

### VI-B Constrained Tracking Across Scenes and Policies
In complex scenes featuring furniture and appliances from RoboCasa, CoFiT was evaluated across two tracking policies: TWIST2 and SONIC. In challenging setups where reference trajectories intersected obstacles, CoFiT reduced violation time by 91% on TWIST2 and 21% on SONIC compared to filter-only training, while lowering correction magnitudes by 59% and 29%, respectively. Simply adding the constraint observations significantly improved policy–filter coordination without compromising tracking accuracy.

### VI-C Real-Robot Validation
On a physical Unitree G1 humanoid performing a forward reaching task around a basketball obstacle, the fine-tuning baseline suffered violent throttling due to policy–filter conflicts as the arm neared the ball, requiring operator stops in 5 out of 10 trials. In contrast, CoFiT completed all 10 trials smoothly without any stops. On TWIST2, violation time dropped by 83%, and residual acceleration was halved from 65.6 to 31.9 rad/s², delivering noticeably smoother whole-body avoidance.

sections.heading: Takeaways and Future Outlook
sections.summary: CoFiT achieves harmony between whole-body tracking policies and runtime safety filters by embedding filter computation data into policy observations, history, and rewards. Future work will explore integration with safety-aware planners.
sections.details: This study presented CoFiT, a filter-aware fine-tuning method that harmonizes pretrained whole-body motion trackers with runtime CBF safety filters. By providing compact action-space constraint representations, intervention histories, and slack-aware penalty rewards, CoFiT drastically cuts constraint violations and eliminates aggressive chattering without sacrificing tracking capability. An important future direction is integrating CoFiT with safety-aware high-level trajectory planners to handle scenarios where paths are completely obstructed and require global detours.

takeaways: Simply appending a safety filter downstream of a tracking policy is not enough; filter interventions conflict with policy dynamics and objectives, triggering severe oscillations.
Constraint normals and margins calculated inside the QP filter serve as remarkably effective action-space observations for the tracking policy.
Providing history feedback on past filter corrections and penalizing QP constraint relaxation (slack) enables policies to learn smooth, coordinated avoidance behaviors.
limitations: CoFiT is designed for whole-body coordination during local interference and near misses; it cannot perform global replanning to circumvent fully obstructed paths on its own.

Only the single most critical constraint (top-1) is passed to the policy, which could provide insufficient information in dense environments where multiple obstacles are simultaneously in close proximity.
Because safety penalties are prioritized, there is a minor trade-off resulting in slightly higher tracking error (MPJPE) relative to the nominal reference trajectory.
